newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nurse's brother feels no choice but to play God.
newsitem.headline: Nurse's brother feels no choice but to play God.

text.p: Stroking his bushy grey beard at the kitchen table of his mother's old house in suburban Adelaide, Frank Gilford says he does not want to play God.

But the 59-year-old parcel courier from a small country town in southern Australia feels he may have no option but to send two British nurses to their death if they are convicted in a Saudi Arabian court of murdering his sister Yvonne.
His big worry, he says, is that if he does not insist on the maximum penalty -- beheading -- they will be let off lightly.
A few years in a Saudi jail and they would be free to return to Britain, sell their story and besmirch his sister's name -- or worse, kill again.
"It seems to be the maximum on one side and nothing on the other, there does not seem to be any middle road," he says.

Gilford has driven with his wife Laurel the few hours south from his home in Jamestown, South Australia, to the house where he last saw his sister, in May 1996, before her official papers to nurse in the rich Islamic nation came through.

He is on his way to visit his 84-year-old mother, Muriel, who suffers from Alzheimer's disease and now lives in a nursing home here, unaware her son has been thrust into an extraordinary legal and moral position since her daughter's death.

The Gilfords will not tell her of the soul-searching they say has gone on for months -- "the agonising, the thoughts, the horror" -- since they learned that, under Saudi law, a murder victim's family can call for death, grant forgiveness or take financial compensation known as blood money.

They will not tell her of the barrage of calls they have taken in the week -- 600 at last count, mainly from Australian and British media -- after the Saudi court hearing the murder case adjourned to allow the accused, Deborah Parry and Lucille McLaughlan, to appeal for mercy.

Instead, they will talk about their children (eight between them from former marriages), their grandchildren, their work, perhaps about Laurel's darts and croquet, Frank's pistol-shooting, their fiddling about on the computer and watching satellite television -- all the minutia of daily life which has been turned upside down in the last six months.

"None of our life is left, everything has completely changed," Gilford says, regretting he has not had the chance to grieve properly for the sister who had planned Saudi Arabia as her last overseas posting to save for her retirement.
"We do not get any peace from the media, the phone is always ringing...trying to find out why you made up your mind, how you made up your mind, are you just out for vengeance," he said.

Pouring cups of coffee, Gilford objects to being portrayed as a hardliner, but the former farm manager then quietly declares the two accused -- whom his wife refers to as "the girls" -- have forfeited their right to being part of the human race.
"If a dog goes out and kills a mob of sheep, what do you do with it? You put it down so it cannot do it again," he said.
Gilford's position remains that he believes the death penalty is the right sentence in the absence of better options.

It is a position he says he has reached through knowing his sister, learning of the savage nature of her death -- she was stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated -- and through stories related by some of people she used to work with.

Gilford describes himself as an average, every day, private person, and while his every word can now make international headlines, he has sought little advice outside his family and the Saudi legal firm which is representing him for no charge.
He does not know if he will take up an offer from Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer to discuss the situation.
And he does not want to read the appeals for mercy from the two accused, who deny the crime, nor to meet their families, saying it can only cause more trauma for both sides.

Yet he is acutely aware of the legal and diplomatic pressure around the case and sees the possibility that Saudi and British authorities could find a compromise, or that the women could be convicted for a lesser crime which would relieve him of a role.

"You have got the Saudis wishing it would go away, you have got the English wishing it would go away, the Australians wishing it would go away, all because there is one lone Australian sticking his bloody hand up," he says.
